papers.title: Parameterisation of NMC and LFP 4680 cells for electrochemical and thermal modelling
papers.abstract: An electrochemical-thermal model of the 4680 cylindrical cell is presented: a Doyle-Fuller-Newman model of the electrode stack coupled to a two-node thermal balance of the roll and the can (a thermal DFN, TDFN), solved by an implicit finite-volume scheme. Two cells are parameterised from teardown geometry and open literature, with every value tagged by provenance: the Tesla NMC811/graphite tabless cell and the BYD FC4680 LiFePO4 multi-tab cell. The reaction heat is evaluated at the open-circuit potential of the particle-mean concentration, which restores the heat of mixing. Both sets are calibrated in the same way, with the test fixture identified from the measurement alone. Against the 1C and 2C charge test of Ank et al., the calibrated NMC set follows the mean can temperature within 0.52 and 1.46 K, with a contact heat of 0.94 mOhm matching the authors' estimate for their holder. For the LFP cell, 1C and 2C discharges to 2.0 V were measured on the authors' bench; the fixture conductance (0.337 W/K) follows from the energy balance and the heat capacity (277 J/K) from the cooling. With the end-of-lithiation drop of LiFePO4 restored in the cathode open-circuit potential, the calibrated set follows the can temperature within 0.44 K (1C) and 0.76 K (2C), reproduces the peaks and the relaxation after cut-off. What remains is what a single can node and a single representative particle do not describe: the axial gradient of the NMC can under contact heating, and a gradual decline of the LFP voltage before the knee at 2C, which points to the distribution of particle states in the electrode. The parameter sets (BPX, CSV) and the bench data are openly available.

papers.title: Improvise, Adapt, Overcome: An On-The-Fly Multifidelity Algorithm for Efficient Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Machine learning has accelerated quantum chemistry but is hindered by the prohibitive cost of generating high fidelity training data. Multifidelity machine learning (MFML) mitigates this overhead by systematically combining abundant low fidelity data with sparse high fidelity data. In spite of its success, standard MFML schemes rely on pre-defined scaling factors to determine sparse data ratio across fidelities, often generating redundant multifidelity data resulting in a loss of efficiency. Here, we introduce an adaptive on-the-fly multifidelity framework for machine learning that autonomously determines training dataset composition. By dynamically querying training samples at each fidelity, the algorithm saturates model accuracy at lower fidelities before moving up to more expensive reference calculations. We benchmark the novel adaptive-MFML across diverse chemical properties including theoretical best estimate ab initio potential energy surfaces, golden standard coupled cluster energies, and the more chemically challenging excitation energies. In our numerical experiments we show that our adaptive algorithm reduces data generation costs by up to a factor of 20 compared to single fidelity methods and improves upon standard MFML by up to a factor of 3. The mitigation of data redundancy establishes a high-accuracy low-cost pathway for sustainable cost-aware machine learning in quantum chemistry.

papers.title: Machine-Learned Compact Subspace Generation for Quantum Selected Configuration Interaction within Density Matrix Embedding Framework
papers.abstract: Sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), an extension of quantum selected configuration interaction (QSCI), is a promising hybrid quantum-classical paradigm for molecular ground-state energies. By replacing variational optimization with quantum sampling, QSCI avoids barren plateaus and directly reconstructs correlated wavefunctions. However, existing configuration recovery mainly enforces symmetry constraints without targeting the most physically relevant configurations, often yielding oversized subspaces and costly classical diagonalization. We introduce QSCI-RBM, a compact subspace generation protocol based on Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs), and integrate it within Density Matrix Embedding Theory (DMET). The RBM learns the distribution of dominant determinants from hardware samples, generating high-probability configurations. Sampling was performed on IBM Heron R1 (\texttt{ibm\_torino}) for CH$_5$NO, R2 (\texttt{ibm\_fez}) for C$_2$H$_4$, and R3 (\texttt{ibm\_boston}) for the larger H$_2$O benchmark and the protein-ligand system. After validating on these benchmarks of increasing active-space size, we simulate the inhibitor Carmofur bound to the SARS-CoV-2 main protease (M\textsuperscript{pro}), fragmented into ten DMET impurities. Both DMET-QSCI-RBM and a DMET-SQD baseline reach chemical-potential self-consistency within four $\mu$-iterations. At the converged chemical potential, DMET-QSCI-RBM lies within $0.05\,\mathrm{mHa}$ of DMET-FCI while accessing on average only $0.22\%$ of the symmetry-preserving configuration space, versus $0.55\,\mathrm{mHa}$ at $33.0\%$ for DMET-SQD, leading to a $\sim$153-fold subspace reduction. RBM-assisted expansion thus yields far more compact hardware-derived determinant spaces at equal or better accuracy, reducing classical overhead for scalable quantum embedding of biological systems on real hardware.

papers.title: PeptSol: A Translational Benchmark for Protected-Peptide Solubility in Drug Manufacturing
papers.abstract: Liquid-phase peptide synthesis (LPPS) offers a scalable route to peptide manufacturing, but route development still depends on empirical solvent screens because each protected intermediate must be soluble for reaction and recoverable for purification. The protecting groups, terminal modifications, and noncanonical residues that govern this behaviour are poorly represented in existing peptide property benchmarks, limiting the ability to develop and rigorously evaluate molecular representation models for LPPS-relevant prediction tasks. We introduce PeptSol, an open benchmark of 1388 hand-curated protected-peptide solubility measurements with chemistry-aware splits. The measurements span only 84 parent sequences and 101 protected structures, and 92.5% come from a single historical programme. Across seven frozen molecular encoders, the best macro-F1 is 0.843 on binary solubility for the historical subset under a peptide-held-out split; the harder three-class ordinal task reaches 0.614 in that cell. No foundation model consistently outperforms a baseline combining chemical fingerprints with explicit molecular descriptors, and model rankings vary across prediction tasks and data splits. The dataset, evaluation protocol, and baselines establish a standard for measuring progress on molecular representations for synthesis-aware peptide developability.

papers.title: Restrained Diffusion Bridges: Targeted Denoiser Training and Refinement
papers.abstract: Diffusion models are often inaccurate in critical, data-sparse regions of the target distribution. Sampling from restrained distributions, biased distributions used in classical enhanced sampling to concentrate data near chosen configurations, can control where training data are collected but biases the learned distribution. We establish that this bias cancels exactly when forward noising from restrained data is conditioned on the restrained configuration at an appropriately chosen intermediate time. This allows a pretrained model fine-tuned on restrained data to achieve high accuracy in any chosen region of the target distribution, regardless of its probability, using standard denoising or flow matching objectives without importance weights. When no target data are available, Gibbs sampling enables inference from a model trained exclusively on restrained data.

papers.title: FlowBatt: Flow Matching for Probabilistic Battery Degradation Prediction
papers.abstract: Battery degradation remains a central challenge in the development and broad application of sustainable energy technologies. Accurate degradation prediction is challenging, as battery aging emerges from complex and heterogeneous interactions among cycling behavior, operating conditions, and cell chemistry. Existing machine-learning approaches typically focus on deterministic end-of-life predictions or modeling degradation curves within fixed chemistry settings, leaving probabilistic state of health (SOH) trajectory modeling across heterogeneous chemistries underexplored. We introduce FlowBatt, a use-inspired conditional generative framework that adapts flow matching with a diffusion transformer (DiT) backbone to battery degradation trajectory modeling. FlowBatt models full SOH trajectories as probabilistic degradation processes conditioned on early-cycle capacity data. To strengthen this conditioning pathway, we use explainable AI analysis to diagnose and improve the encoder that maps early-cycle capacity matrices into conditioning vectors. We evaluate FlowBatt on five public benchmark settings spanning diverse chemistries and aging conditions, comparing it with supervised and diffusion-based trajectory models as well as established baselines for remaining useful life (RUL) prediction under shared data splits. FlowBatt achieves the best trajectory-wise SOH prediction performance on all five datasets, with errors below 2.5%, and delivers competitive RUL prediction performance. By generating multiple plausible trajectories, FlowBatt provides empirical prediction intervals for battery degradation modeling. These results indicate that flow-matching-based trajectory modeling is a promising framework for probabilistic battery health prediction.

papers.title: VESPER: Online Learning of Free Energies with a Multi-Tempered Variational Objective
papers.abstract: Computing molecular free-energy landscapes over collective variables (CVs) is central to understanding molecular mechanisms, but poses a difficult learning problem without training data available a priori. Samples of the marginal CV distribution must be generated by molecular dynamics (MD), whose trajectories can remain trapped in metastable states and rarely cross the free-energy barriers governing conformational changes or chemical reactions. We introduce VESPER, which couples the generation of these samples to neural-network-driven free-energy learning: MD supplies configurations for learning, while the evolving model biases the MD to accelerate exploration and generate further training data. VESPER minimizes a single variational objective that is convex in the free energy and can combine several tempering levels, each flattening the free-energy landscape to promote barrier crossing. Every level has the same physical free energy as its minimizer, allowing data from all levels to train one shared model without reweighting. Learning uses the difference in mean parameter gradients between biased MD configurations and auxiliary walkers that explore the flattened model in CV space. We prove conditional convergence of the coupled overdamped population dynamics without replica exchange under log-Sobolev and Polyak-Lojasiewicz assumptions. VESPER matches or improves on established enhanced-sampling methods on alanine dipeptide and yields self-consistent free-energy reconstructions from three to six CVs on alanine tetrapeptide. For methane dehydrogenation on Ni(511) with a machine-learned interatomic potential, it recovers two-CV Boltzmann marginals and a reactant-to-saddle free-energy difference along a three-CV path, both qualitatively consistent with the lower-dimensional reference. It also samples RMSD-defined folded and unfolded regions of chignolin while biasing seventeen CVs.

papers.title: Neural network approximation of regularized density functionals
papers.abstract: We study neural-network approximation of density functionals in a Banach-space setting. Since the exact continuum functionals are discontinuous in the natural density topology, we apply $p$-Moreau-Yosida regularization. We construct finite-rank ReLU networks that preserve convexity and nonnegativity, lie below the regularized functional, and approximate it uniformly on compact sets. For energies obtained by minimization over compact density sets, we account exactly for the energy shift caused by regularization and bound the remaining error by the localization on these compact sets and network approximation errors. We apply this framework to canonical and grand-canonical density-functional theory at fixed particle number and fixed mean particle number, respectively. We obtain uniform energy convergence on norm-compact classes of external potentials, including molecular Coulomb potentials. We illustrate our results through numerical experiments on a simple model system.

papers.title: Density functionals for the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian
papers.abstract: We develop a density-functional theory for the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian of nonrelativistic quantum electrodynamics in the spirit of the convex-analytic formulation of Lieb. We consider finitely many electrons, subject to external scalar and vector potentials, coupled to the full continuum of massless transverse photons with an ultraviolet cutoff. The natural basic variables are the standard electron density and a combined current density, the sum of the paramagnetic current density and a field-induced current density generated by the quantized vector potential. We prove representability results for these density-current pairs and show that the mixed-state constrained-search functional attains its infimum and coincides with the Lieb functional obtained by convex conjugation. Since arbitrarily soft photons purify mixed states at a negligible energy cost without changing their density and combined current density, the pure-state Levy-Lieb functional equals the Lieb functional and is therefore convex, even though its infimum need not be attained. In addition, we establish the zero-coupling limit, which recovers the mixed-state Vignale-Rasolt functional of current-density-functional theory. Finally, we consider the long-wavelength (dipole) limit and show that the limiting functional can be written as a constrained search for the well-known length-gauge dipole Hamiltonian.

papers.title: Optimal Control of Chemical Reaction Networks with Thermodynamic Cost
papers.abstract: Thermodynamic control seeks to realize desired functions at minimal thermodynamic cost, yet existing frameworks remain largely confined to slow driving regimes or state-to-state transport. Here we establish a thermodynamic optimal-control theory for Markov jump processes (MJPs) and chemical reaction networks (CRNs) that accommodates objectives over both states and reaction fluxes beyond slow-driving limit. By deriving the thermodynamic Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equation, we demonstrate that the optimal dynamics take the form of a perturbed generalized-gradient flow driven by the value function. A convex representation of the entropy-production rate via generalized means identifies its Legendre--Fenchel dual as the dissipation function. The resulting dynamics shares the thermodynamic structure of CRNs and admits an information-geometric characterization. We further derive a thermodynamic Pontryagin equation by recasting the control problem in terms of thermodynamic forces, providing a complementary description of optimal trajectories and clarifying connections to thermodynamic optimal transport. Our results establish a thermodynamic and geometric foundation for controlling MJPs and CRNs beyond mere transport, opening avenues for optimizing biological processes and finite-time thermodynamic operations in far-from-equilibrium regimes.

papers.title: Impact of Surface Preparation on the Propulsion of Catalytic Janus Colloids and Implications for Reproducibility
authors: Christopher L. Wirth (Case Western Reserve University)
papers.abstract: Platinum-coated polystyrene (PS) Janus particles (JPs) propelled by the catalytic decomposition of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) are a widely used model system for active matter, yet reported speeds for similar particles and fuel concentrations differ by more than an order of magnitude. Broad adoption of these materials requires increasing consistency in the preparation and achieving improved repeatability in their behavior. Herein, we focused on two routine, but rarely reported, preparation steps that we found to alter the particle speed. First, we found that pre-exposing the platinum cap to H2O2 before cell assembly increased the mean speed by a factor of 2.4. The size of this effect depended on batch history, where an aged batch responded strongly, while a freshly prepared batch sped up by only 16%. Second, we found that plasma cleaning of the glass substrate decreased the speed 2.7 times. In a 120 $\mu$m cell the suppression was the same at both walls even when only one wall was treated. The suppression grew with the treated glass area per unit fluid volume, which pointed to species released into the bulk solution rather than to a change at the wall. Plasma-cleaned glass released more ions into water than untreated glass, and XPS detected an ionic metal fluoride on the plasma-cleaned surface. A model in which the released ions lower the speed through the solution conductivity reproduced the measured speeds in all four cell geometries. Of the 17 published studies compared here, pre-activation is reported in only four studies and substrate cleaning in only six studies. We propose a minimum reporting standard for the preparation and associated speed measurements of catalytic Janus particles.

papers.title: Dysfunctional Functionals and their Therapies in Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory
papers.abstract: The exchange-correlation functional in Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory (TDDFT) is known to have dependence on past densities and initial states, and yet this memory-dependence is ignored in practical calculations which almost always use an adiabatic approximation. We discuss the dysfunction that arises due to this deficiency and point to therapies that go beyond the adiabatic approximation. Still, adiabatic TDDFT has had success in a wide range of systems for response properties and for fully non-equilibrium dynamics, and why this is so is only partially understood. This, together with the rigorous foundation of the exact theory and its favorable system-size scaling, provides tremendous impetus for continuing to strive towards improved approximations to the exact functionals, and a deeper understanding of the impact of approximations in applications.

papers.title: Graph-Covariant Bottom-Up Scale-Bridging Reconstruction of Ground and Excited States of Extended Systems
papers.abstract: We propose a hierarchical scale-bridging construction for building first principles electronic structure models of extended molecular aggregates with disorder, and its practical realization in exciton systems. The general construction, referred here as to the encapsulation, is based on a recursive operator-valued hierarchy cast in a dual graph-theoretic (discrete) and configuration-space (continuous) structure, in which variables associated with a coarser level parameterize operators governing the degrees of freedom at the next finer level in a graph-covariant, geometry-preserving fashion. In an exemplary application of this scheme, aggregate-level ground- and excited-state operators are constructed through a many-body expansion (MBE), with matrix elements evaluated in a basis comprising the aggregate ground state and local Frenkel excitations. The required monomer and dimer building blocks are obtained from DFT and TDDFT calculations, yielding aggregate-level 1-particle transition density matrices as well as Hamiltonian, dipole moment and other operators that can be evaluated at the level of the building blocks. Starting from structural models obtained from experiment or molecular dynamics, this approach generates aggregate-level operators in a bottom-up fashion without fitting parameters to spectroscopic data or performing calculations on larger system cutouts. A numerical demonstration is given for an excitonic manifold in crystalline quaterthiophene. In particular, through its intrinsic configuration-dependence encoded in the encapsulations, it will provide a bridge between static electronic structure calculations for realistic, structurally disordered aggregates and quantum or quantum-classical simulations of exciton-vibrational dynamics.

papers.title: Unlocking n-alk-1-ynes Conformers: Quantum "Trigger Finger" versus "Stiff Joint" Conformations
papers.abstract: Molecular conformation in n-alk-1-ynes (CnA) is conventionally simplified to an all-planar structure. We report a comprehensive quantum chemical analysis revealing two near-isoenergetic rotamers at the acetylenic terminus: planar (C$_s$) and skewed (C$_1$). The high, symmetric rotational energy barrier ($\approx 150$\,meV) arises from unique steric relief near the $\mathrm{sp}$ center coupled with electronic stabilization of C$_1$. This creates a unique kinetic profile: a Quantum ``Trigger Finger'' ($\alpha$ rotation) that enforces an $\approx 50\%:\,50\%$ $\mathrm{C}_s/\mathrm{C}_1$ ensemble, sharply contrasting with the thermodynamically biased ``Stiff Joint'' ($\delta$ rotation) of the alkyl chain. This structural degeneracy necessitates ensemble averaging for spectroscopic data interpretation, while the slow interconversion permits kinetic trapping and intentional conformer enrichment during synthesis and molecular junction fabrication. Our work redefines the alkyne anchor, providing a blueprint for accurate interpretation of spectroscopic data and achieving conformational control in molecular electronics.

papers.title: All-electron Dynamical Bethe-Salpeter Equation for Extended Systems with Atom-centered Orbital Basis
papers.abstract: Solving Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) for the two-particle Green's function is the most widely used approach for taking into account the particle-hole (exciton) interaction in electronic excitation in the context of the many-body theory based on Green's function. In BSE calculations, the static approximation to the screened Coulomb interaction kernel is commonly employed. However, when the excitonic character is significant as typically indicated by a large exciton binding energy, dynamical screening effects become non-negligible, rendering the static approximation questionable. Because of the large computational cost due to the dense Brillouin zone integration necessary for convergence, solving the dynamical BSE for extended systems remains a significant challenge, especially when combined with GW calculation for the calculation of quasi-particle energies. In this work, we formulate the plane-wave based effective dielectric function method [Zhang, et al., Phys. Rev. B 107, 235205 (2023)] for the dynamical BSE calculation using atom-centered orbitals as basis functions. We implement this approach in our recently developed all-electron numerical atom-centered orbital (NAO) implementation of BSE@GW [Zhou, et. al. J. Chem. Theory Comput. 21, 291 (2025)] for extended systems. We validate our all-electron NAO-based implementation of the dynamical BSE method, and we then discuss its realistic application to molecular crystal of naphthalene by performing the dynamical BSE@G0W0 calculation.

papers.title: Intermolecular and Interfacial Origins of Layering in a Near-Isotropic Organic Glass Former
papers.abstract: Physical vapor deposition can produce organic glasses with enhanced stability and pronounced structural anisotropy (layering) even when the constituent molecules are nearly spherical. However, the microscopic origin of the layering in spherical molecular glass formers remains unclear. We investigated vapor-deposited films of 9-(3,5-di(naphthalen-1-yl)phenyl)anthracene ({\alpha},{\alpha}-A) by grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering, atomistic molecular dynamics, and coarse-grained simulations. Experimentally, the layering signal varies nonmonotonically with deposition temperature and is strongest near 0.8T_g. Simulated scattering calculations reproduce the principal experimental features and show that the layering peak does not originate from shifts in single molecule degrees of freedom. In fact, the simulated deposited and bulk glasses show largely the same single-molecule conformations. Interestingly, a one-site coarse-grained liquid with isotropic interactions develops a comparable interfacial layering signature. These results indicate that layering in {\alpha},{\alpha}-A arises primarily from collective density correlations generated at the free surface during deposition rather than from conformational bias or orientational ordering. The findings connect structural anisotropy in vapor-deposited molecular glasses to the generic interfacial organization of simple liquids.

papers.title: From First Bond to Stable Adhesion: Multivalent Bond Stabilization in Receptor-Mediated Endocytosis
papers.abstract: After a particle forms its first receptor--ligand bond near a cell membrane, stable attachment often requires a threshold number of additional bonds. This paper develops a biophysical kinetic theory of this post-capture stage. The bond-number dynamics are modeled as a finite birth--death chain on $n=0,1,\dots,m$, where $0$ is loss of the initial bond and $m$ is the stabilization threshold. The mesoscopic rates $\lambda_n$ and $\mu_n$ encode the local energy landscape, accessible receptor--ligand pairs, steric and orientational constraints, and cooperative interactions within the growing cluster. The probability of reaching the threshold before losing the first bond is derived in closed form for general rates and, in the constant-ratio case, reduces to a geometric series controlled by the free-energy bias $\rho_n=\mu_n/\lambda_n$. The mean time to failure or stabilization follows from a tridiagonal backward equation. Conditioning on successful attachment is treated as a trajectory-selection effect: the conditioned chain is a Doob $h$-transform whose dissociation rate at $n=1$ vanishes, because successful trajectories cannot lose the first bond early. A minimal interface between the spatial first-capture probability and the bond-number chain is formulated, together with the conditions under which the stable capture probability factorizes into their product. The analysis shows that hitting probabilities constrain only the rate ratios, whereas the absolute rate scale requires time-resolved or dwell-time data. The threshold $m$ is a model-defined stabilization criterion, not a directly measured ligand count. The rates and threshold are effective parameters specified independently or inferred from kinetic data. The theory provides a quantitative framework for interpreting attachment probabilities, lifetimes, and the transition from first bond formation to stable multivalent adhesion.

papers.title: Before the First Bond: Depletion-Assisted Stochastic Capture at the Onset of Endocytosis
papers.abstract: In a crowded extracellular environment, viruses and nanoparticles must reach the cell membrane within a few nanometers before the first ligand-receptor bond can form. Crowders generate an entropic depletion attraction, yet continuum models usually assume contact is already established or treat the approach deterministically. We formulate a thermodynamically consistent stochastic theory for this pre-contact stage. The sphere-plane depletion geometry uses the exact Asakur-Oosawa spherical-cap overlap, rather than a fitted cap, with either ideal van 't Hoff or pressure-only Carnahan-Starling osmotic pressure. A spatially varying near-wall mobility introduces a noise-induced drift that is essential for thermodynamic consistency and is often omitted. The first specific reaction is modeled by a Robin radiation boundary; the outer boundary is reflecting or absorbing. Three first-passage problems are solved analytically by quadrature: the mean reaction time, the reaction-before-escape probability, and the conditional success time, the last encoded by a Doob transform that exposes the selection bias of conditioning on capture. The theory separates thermodynamic inputs from conditional parameters and reveals a reaction-limited to diffusion-limited crossover controlled by the local Damk\"ohler number. For typical virus and nanoparticle parameters, the depletion well reaches $2$-$6\,k_{\rm B}T$, capture times are $0.1$-$1\,{\rm ms}$, and the conditional success time is measurably shorter than the unconditional mean. Finite-volume and Chebyshev schemes reproduce the analytic results within their discretization errors and satisfy the radiation-boundary mass balance. This provides a quantitative theoretical framework for crowding-assisted capture prior to membrane wrapping and a reference for comparing crowding, near-wall mobility, and surface reactivity in endocytosis.

papers.title: Valence-Selective Electrophoretic Transport in Neutral Carbon Nanotubes
papers.abstract: Understanding how confinement alters the transport of charged molecules is central to the advancement of separation, energy, and sensing technologies. Polyamines are small, linear molecules with ionizable groups, making them an ideal model for investigating charge transport in confinement beyond monatomic ions. Using all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, we investigate how molecular length, net charge, and charge placement affect the electrophoretic transport of polyamines through single-walled carbon nanotubes (CNTs). We find that nanometer-scale confinement reverses the mobility ordering observed in free solution -- in a CNT of radius 0.68 nm, spermine (q = +4) travels more slowly than ethylamine (q = +1), contrasting with the expected scaling of mobility with valence in bulk. Further, we find that mobility decreases faster than the inverse of valence, though molecular size and length vary alongside this trend. Comparisons of doubly protonated spermidine microspecies reveal the additional influence of charge placement at fixed net valence. Upon moving one proton of dicationic spermidine from the central to a terminal nitrogen, the mobility is increased by 42%. We analyze hydration structure and solute-solvent association, identifying local-solvation differences between protonation topologies that accompany these distinct transport responses under confinement. These results suggest that neutral CNTs could support valence-selective nanofluidic transport, with additional sensitivity to molecular structure and protonation topology.

papers.title: Extended Onsager's variational principle for nonlinear chemical reaction kinetics in active matter
papers.abstract: Onsager's variational principle (OVP) constructs dissipative dynamics from free energy, dissipation, and input power, but deterministic rate laws alone do not identify fluctuations or chemical fuel consumption. We examine these distinctions for nonlinear reaction kinetics in active matter. Comparing Gaussian diffusion and Poisson reaction events clarifies when statistical fluctuations match a physical Rayleighian: the reaction dissipation potential must be consistent with counting statistics, local detailed balance links rate bias to chemical affinity, and kinetic scales remain constitutive inputs. Under these conditions, the normalized Rayleighian excess gives the leading rate-fluctuation cost in the frozen-state, many-event regime. Three models illustrate the consequences. Spatially uniform reactions exhibit protocol-dependent nonreciprocal response compatible with fixed-state OVP; different Rayleighian representations can select the same rate without specifying the same fluctuations. In an active emulsion, a finite fuel pool accounts for free-energy transfer and dissolution of a chemically maintained domain after replenishment stops. In a membrane-cytosol model, distinct reaction-channel realizations yield identical protein-density trajectories but different chemical input power. Under a separate kinetic assumption, an exact total-density equation still requires an initial rate and does not determine chemical work or fluctuations. These results clarify the physical and statistical inputs required for constructing reaction-transport models and interpreting their fluctuations.

papers.title: An Electrolyte Equation of State Based on openCOSMO-RS: From Aqueous Solutions to Non-Aqueous Systems
papers.abstract: Predictive COSMO-RS-based electrolyte models such as COSMO-RS-ES describe electrolyte solutions from quantum-chemical information, but treat the liquid as incompressible and give no access to densities or pressure effects. This work presents openCOSMO-RS-ES-Phi, to our knowledge the first open-source implementation of a predictive electrolyte equation of state based on openCOSMO-RS. It combines the COSMO-RS-based equation of state openCOSMO-RS-Phi with the ion interaction energies and the long-range term of COSMO-RS-ES, which is first refitted on the same simplified short range. With this refit, a dielectric decrement improves the mean ionic activity coefficients (MIAC), whereas a Born term counts the solvation of the ions a second time and is therefore left out. The equation of state then adds only volume, dispersion and temperature parameters of the ions, fitted to aqueous MIAC and densities. openCOSMO-RS-ES-Phi reproduces COSMO-RS-ES in dilute aqueous solutions, improves on it in concentrated ones and also yields solution densities. Extrapolating from aqueous systems, it predicts the MIAC in water + cosolvent mixtures as accurately as the fitted COSMO-RS-ES, as well as the MIAC and bubble points of a benchmark database of water-alcohol-salt systems. Salting-out of organic components is not described as accurately, and salts come out too soluble in organic solvents. Overall, the interaction model developed for COSMO-RS-ES carries over to a large extent to an equation of state, which makes openCOSMO-RS-ES-Phi a sound base model for further development, with ion transfer between solvents as a clear target for fitting to non-aqueous data.

papers.title: Flame Bifurcation, Flashback Margins, and NOx Scaling in a Swirl-Stabilized Hydrogen Aero-Engine Combustor
papers.abstract: Burning neat hydrogen in aircraft turbines eliminates carbon emissions, yet rapid reaction rates trigger nozzle flashback hazards and high nitrogen oxide emissions across flight throttles. This study investigates aerothermal holding mechanisms, flashback safety margins, and emission pathways in a dual-swirl combustor across equivalence ratios from 0.55 to 1.00. Three-dimensional simulations combine curvature-corrected shear-stress transport turbulence closure, dual-rate finite-rate and eddy-dissipation chemical kinetics, and discrete ordinates radiation, validated against experimental laser benchmarks using ASME grid standards. Advancing engine throttle triggers a topological flame bifurcation from a faceplate-attached M-flame at lean idle to a lifted V-flame above equivalence ratio 0.895, while wall flashback safety indices consistently exceed 3.42. Nitric oxide emissions transition from water-chaperoned nitrous oxide intermediate reactions at lean idle (28.01 ppm, EINOx = 1.85 g/kg), scaling to 319.21 ppm (EINOx = 35.40 g/kg) at takeoff under thermal Zeldovich dominance, governed by a power-law exponent of 4.92. These findings deliver validated operability limits and establish an accessible workstation-based screening methodology for practical zero-carbon aero-engine combustor development.

papers.title: Molecular conical intersections with odd electron number are realizations of the topological Yang monopole
papers.abstract: The two-level conical intersection of a molecule with odd electron number in the absence of magnetic field obeys time-reversal symmetry $T^{2}=-1$ (referred to as the $T^{2}=-1$ conical intersection), and has a five-dimensional branching space due to the Kramer degeneracy. Similar to how the conical intersection of a molecule in a magnetic field ($T^{2}=0$) behaves as the Dirac monopole, the $T^{2}=-1$ conical intersection behaves as the Yang monopole, an mathematical generalization of Dirac monopole with SU(2) gauge field and SO(5) symmetry. This implies that we can study topological properties of $T^{2}=-1$ conical intersections in chemistry based on what is known about Yang monopole in high energy physics. In this work, we present a few mathematical tools to study this connection. First, we show that geometric algebra and quaternion numbers together provides a natural way to utilize the $T^{2}=-1$ time reversal symmetry and the SO(5) symmetry in scaled coordinates, making it simple to derive eigenfunctions, Berry connection and Berry curvature of $T^{2}=-1$ conical intersection. In particular, this approach provides a simple proof that when viewed from the upper or lower states, the $T^{2}=-1$ conical intersection behaves as the self-dual or self-antidual Yang monopole with second Chern number $C_{2}=+\frac{1}{4}$ or $-\frac{1}{4}$ respectively. In addition, we propose a visualization method for the SU(2) Berry connection of $T^{2}=-1$ conical intersection. This is achieved by showing that the nonzero part of the Berry connection induces Hopf-fibration on the $S^{3}$ longitude space, and is further visualized through stereographic projection.

papers.title: Simple algorithm for evaluating SU(2) non-abelian geometric phase in the vicinity of molecular conical intersection of odd electron number
papers.abstract: Molecular conical intersection of odd-electron number are known to give arise to non-abelian geometric phases. In this work, we present a simple algorithm for evaluating the SU(2) geometric phases given a trajectory represented as a discrete set of coordinates in the 5-dimensional branching space. Motivated by the special property that such conical intersection behaves as abelian ones in 3-dimensional subspace, we take two steps to establish the algorithm. We first prove that it is possible to construct an augmented trajectory consisting of spherical triangles that has the same geometric phases as the original trajectory. We then prove that the geometric phase contribution from each spherical triangle can be evaluated from its properties using Stokes' theorem in a way that closely resembles abelian conical intersections. The total geometric phases are thus evaluated by path-ordered products of contributions from each spherical triangle. Based on the augmented trajectory, we further show that the geometric phases of the upper and lower states will switch under inversion transformation of the trajectory. This relation is further generalized to show that the Wilson loop, defined as the trace of the geometric phases, will switch between the two states under any 5-dimensional improper isometric transformation. Example calculations of geometric phases for trajectories generated on 5-dimensional polytopes are also presented and discussed.

papers.title: PLUMED-JAX: GPU-native enhanced sampling for atomistic simulations
papers.abstract: We present PLUMED-JAX, an AI-assisted adaptation of selected PLUMED collective variables, umbrella sampling, and metadynamics for JAX-based atomistic simulations, developed using gpt-6.1-sol with reasoning effort set to high within the Codex harness. Integration with JAX-MD supports compiled molecular dynamics, batched replicas, walkers sharing a bias, and execution across multiple graphics processing units. We validate the framework against PLUMED and exact free energy benchmarks, and demonstrate applications to butane, silicon crystallization, and lithium transport, with severalfold improvements in computational throughput for both classical forcefields and machine learning interatomic potentials.

papers.title: ROSE: Deep Learning exchange-correlation functional from reduced density-matrix representations
papers.abstract: We introduce ROSE, a deep-learning exchange--correlation energy functional built from the occupied-state density matrix. On GMTKN55 and on additional external benchmarks considered in this work, ROSE improves over modern neural network functionals trained under matched protocols and is on average more accurate than, or on par with, most hybrid and range-separated hybrid functionals considered here. On the experimental benchmarks considered here it has leading accuracy across hybrids, range separated hybrids, and neural functionals. These results motivate nonlocal density-matrix representations as a route to systematic improvement of learned XC functionals with low computational cost.

papers.title: Energy Transfer and Strong Coupling in Plasmonic Systems
papers.abstract: The coupling between plasmon resonances of metal nanostructures and electronic excitations of molecular/semiconductor systems is important in a number of applications, including surface enhanced spectroscopy, hot-electron catalysis, plasmon-induced resonance energy transfer and the creation of hybrid light-matter states. The past several decades has seen a large number of experimental studies of these effects, as well as the development of theory to explain the results. In this Perspectives article we use classical electromagnetic (EM) simulations to examine how the localized surface plasmon resonances (LSPRs) of metal nanoparticles and propagating surface plasmon polaritons (SPPs) in extended metal nanostructures (wires/plates/films) are affected by interactions with a molecular/semiconductor system. The classical EM simulations are complemented by a quantum model for plasmon-exciton coupling based on the macroscopic quantum electrodynamics (MQED) framework, along with Holstein vibrations. The goals are to show how LSPR spectra and SPP dispersion curves/attenuation constants changes as the strength of the molecular/semiconductor electronic transition increases and the system evolves from an energy transfer limit to strong coupling, and to provide an understanding of the decay processes from both classical EM and MQED perspectives.

papers.title: Modeling and Experimental Validation of Bubble-Induced Performance Losses in Microstructured Copper Electrodes for Alkaline Water Electrolysis
papers.abstract: Water electrolysis is a promising technology for sustainable hydrogen (H$_2$) production. However, gas bubble formation significantly degrades the electrochemical surface area ($A_{\rm EC}$) and the electrocatalytic activity of microstructured electrodes in water electrolyzer cells. Existing theoretical models fail to connect computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and electrochemistry to analyze how bubble dynamics affect the performance of gas-evolving microstructured electrodes. This work develops a multiphysics-based theoretical model that couples two-phase CFD with Butler-Volmer and Faradaic kinetics, incorporating exchange current density, cell current, gravitational acceleration, surface tension, and fluid properties such as density and viscosity. The model quantifies essential electrochemical parameters, such as the enhancement in $A_{\rm EC}$ and the overpotential ($\eta$), which deviate by less than 7\% and 15\%, respectively, from the experimental results. Evaluations of the fabricated microstructured electrodes using polarization curves, cyclic voltammetry, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, and linear polarization resistance techniques demonstrate reduced $\eta$ by 2.49--21.39\% and 9.55--24.32\% for oxygen (O$_2$) and H$_2$ evolution, respectively. Furthermore, the model reveals the interplay between enhanced geometric surface area and bubble-transport limitations, facilitating the optimization and analysis of structural parameters. These findings establish a physics-informed roadmap for designing optimal, robust, and industry-scalable microstructured electrodes for efficient H$_2$ generation via water electrolysis.

papers.title: GPU infrastructure for ML/MM with electrostatic embedding for enzyme chemistry
papers.abstract: We present a fully GPU-native framework for machine learning/molecular mechanics (ML/MM) enhanced sampling simulations with electrostatic embedding, demonstrated on an enzymatic reaction. The framework combines a JAX port of the pretrained MACE-POLAR-1-M model, an electrostatic embedding scheme compatible with the MACE-POLAR architecture, and integration with JAX-MD and PLUMED-JAX for end-to-end compiled enhanced sampling. The implementation is developed using GPT-6.1-Sol within Codex, with reasoning effort set to high. Using replica exchange umbrella sampling, we calculate the free energy profile of nucleophilic substitution in haloalkane dehalogenase in approximately 200 H100 GPU hours, treating the entire protein and reactants with MACE-POLAR-1-M-JAX and most of the solvent with molecular mechanics.

papers.title: Relativistic Kohn--Sham Theory of Paramagnetic Magnetic-Resonance Properties
papers.abstract: A general density functional theory based relativistic theory for paramagnetic NMR (pNMR) shifts, EPR g-tensors and hyperfine coupling tensors as well as magnetizabilities is derived. The formulation uses spin--orbit exact two-component (X2C) theory, gauge-including atomic orbitals, and generalized complex Kohn--Sham response equations with all ingredients being implemented analytically with the help of Goldstone modes and an orientation-constrained shielding. Additionally, we describe a two-component augmented Roothaan--Hall (ARH) solver for robust and stable convergence, which ensures that both a stationary point and a minimum are found. This is crucial for the convergence of the response equations for properties of paramagnetic systems. The extension of common population analyses for the two-component theory to aid in the interpretation of the spectra is further described. Using these new techniques, we are able to analyze the success and failure of density functional theory for relativistic open-shell systems including actinide complexes.
